summary: Defines the Local Mail Transfer Protocol, a variation on SMTP for handing mail to a final delivery system without a mail queue. SMTP servers must manage queues, which is unnecessary for plain local delivery.

plainLanguage.summary: LMTP is a variation of SMTP for delivering mail to a system that does not manage its own queue. After message data arrives, the server reports a result separately for each accepted recipient.

questions: how does lmtp differ from smtp
subtitle: A mail-transfer protocol that returns a separate delivery result for each recipient.

tldr.problem: SMTP returns one final reply for a message with multiple recipients, so a delivery server may need to queue and retry recipients with temporary failures.
tldr.mechanism: LMTP replaces HELO or EHLO with LHLO and returns one final DATA reply for each previously accepted recipient.
tldr.outcome: LMTP lets a client manage retries when delivering to systems without queues; it is for prior arrangements and must not use TCP port 25.

facts.label: Reply when no RCPT succeeds before DATA

today: RFC 2033 is an Informational memo published in October 1996, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC states that it does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Local Mail Delivery Needs LMTP
sections.content:
In SMTP, a mail transaction can include several recipients, but the server sends one reply after the message data. If delivery succeeds for some recipients and temporarily fails for others, that single reply cannot report each outcome. SMTP therefore requires the server to manage a queue and retry delivery.

RFC 2033 describes limited situations where a receiver should not need its own queue, such as a local delivery agent. LMTP allows the client to keep responsibility for retrying recipients whose delivery did not succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP gives one final result for a message, even when it has several recipients. LMTP gives a separate result for each accepted recipient so the client can manage retries.

sections.title: Where LMTP Fits
sections.content:
The memo describes a mail system with a queue manager and delivery agents. The queue manager communicates with other hosts using SMTP and stores mail in a persistent queue. Delivery agents handle addresses for which the host accepts responsibility, such as passing mail to another mail system or placing it in a local spool.

LMTP is useful on connections from the queue manager to delivery agents that do not manage queues. The RFC says it is not beneficial when sending mail to the queue manager, because that system already accepts responsibility for later delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: LMTP is intended for a queue manager handing mail to a delivery system that does not keep a queue. The queue manager remains responsible for retrying temporary failures.

sections.title: The LHLO Greeting
sections.content:
LMTP otherwise uses SMTP syntax and service extensions with the changes described in the memo. It replaces the SMTP HELO and EHLO commands with LHLO, which has the same semantics as EHLO. The distinct greeting helps detect when the two sides are configured to use different protocols.

An LMTP server must not return a positive-completion reply to HELO or EHLO. The memo recommends reply code 500 for those commands.
sections.plainLanguage: LMTP uses LHLO as its greeting instead of SMTP's HELO or EHLO. This difference helps the client and server detect a protocol mismatch.

sections.title: A Final Reply for Each Recipient
sections.content:
If no RCPT command succeeded, DATA must fail with reply code 503. Otherwise, after the final dot ending DATA, the server returns one reply for each successful RCPT, in the order the commands were issued. Repeated successful commands for the same recipient still each receive a reply.

A positive-completion reply means the server accepts responsibility for delivering or relaying the message to that recipient. If a connection closes before all replies arrive, the client processes replies already received and treats the remaining recipients as temporary failures.
sections.plainLanguage: After the message data, the server replies once for each accepted recipient, in order. The client uses each reply to decide whether to deliver again later.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Limits
sections.content:
LMTP must not be used on TCP service port 25, and the RFC says it should be used only by specific prior arrangement and configuration. Servers must implement the PIPELINING and ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES extensions; they should implement 8BITMIME. The memo recommends against using LMTP over wide area networks.

Servers should send each recipient's reply as soon as possible, and clients should process replies as they arrive. If only some replies arrive before a connection closes, the client must treat the rest as temporary failures. The RFC states that it has no known security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: LMTP is for configured delivery arrangements, not general mail exchange on TCP port 25. Clients must handle a lost connection by retrying recipients that have no reply.
